issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette:
For fifty years, Omar's hands had known the language of stone. At seventy-five, he still felt most himself in his dusty, sunlit studio, the sharp scent of marble dust in the air, the solid weight of a chisel in his palm. That changed six months ago. He was working on a large commission, a swirling abstract form, and had climbed a short stepladder to refine the upper curve. He remembers a sudden, disorienting wave of dizziness, a sensation of the floor tilting away from him. The fall was short but brutal. He landed awkwardly against a discarded block of granite, the impact sending a sickening, white-hot shock through his hip. Lying on the cold concrete, unable to move, the most terrifying thing was not the pain, but the profound sense of betrayal by his own body, which had failed him without any warning.

The surgery to repair his fractured hip was successful, and the physical therapists praised his recovery. But a deeper injury had taken hold. Omar had come to believe that the fall was not a simple accident but a definitive verdict. He was convinced that his body was no longer a reliable vessel but a fragile, damaged thing, waiting for the next opportunity to collapse. He would tell his daughter, with a quiet, unshakeable certainty, "I have permanently changed for the worse." This conviction became the lens through which he saw everything. He felt as though the fall had exposed a fundamental weakness, a permanent vulnerability that had always been lurking beneath the surface. His body, he was certain, had been permanently damaged by what happened, and he could no longer trust it to carry him through the day.

This core belief that his body was broken and untrustworthy began to govern his every action. He developed a routine of constant, anxious vigilance, a desperate attempt to preempt the next catastrophe. Several times an hour, he would press his fingers to his wrist, counting the beats, checking for the flutter he was sure would precede a heart attack. He'd take deep, deliberate breaths, monitoring for any catch or shallowness that might signal a failing in his lungs. This obsessive body monitoring was exhausting, but it felt necessary-a crucial defense against the internal enemy he now lived with. He also began to avoid any situation that might put his body under what he perceived as stress. This, tragically, meant avoiding his studio. The thought of lifting even a small mallet, of standing for hours to work the stone, now felt like an invitation to disaster. The physical exertion he once thrived on now seemed like a reckless gamble he could not afford to take.

Over the months, this avoidance hardened into a new way of life. His world shrank to the confines of his armchair. Dust gathered on his tools and the half-finished sculptures that filled his studio, monuments to a life he no longer felt capable of living. When not consumed by checking his body for signs of danger, his mind would turn inward, circling the same unanswerable question: "Why has this happened to me?" He would spend hours replaying the fall, searching for a meaning, a reason, a cosmic explanation for this sudden and total decline. It was as if finding a reason would give him some semblance of control, but the question only ever led back to the terrifying belief in his own fragility. The less he did physically, the more he became convinced of his body's decay, and the more certain he was of this decay, the more he retreated from the world. His daughter, visiting one afternoon, found him sitting in the growing dusk, having not eaten all day for fear of the effort of walking to the kitchen. It was the sight of his powerful, capable hands lying limp in his lap, and the profound loss of purpose in his eyes, that finally prompted him to seek help.
